findings.summary: RN 0.85.3 runs Hermes V1 250829098.0.10 on both iOS and Android by default. I built a JSI host against the macOS slice of that exact framework and ran everything in it. Its Intl has only getCanonicalLocales, Collator, DateTimeFormat and NumberFormat. PluralRules, DisplayNames, RelativeTimeFormat, ListFormat, Locale, Segmenter, formatRange, and NumberFormat.formatToParts on iOS are all missing. Hermes source at the tag, the iOS slice strings and the Android AAR classes and .so show the same set on both platforms. Assumption (2) holds: PluralRules is missing, and i18next 26 then picks wrong plural forms silently ('5 minuty' instead of '5 minut' in Polish, verified end-to-end) without logging anything. v26 has no compatibilityJSON fallback left. But the specific npm package intl-pluralrules@2.0.1 is wrong as-is. It feeds grouped strings like '1,021' to make-plural, giving 1614 of 55,560 wrong results against V8/ICU 78 (lt, lv, mt and ro for numbers of 1000 and up; es/fr/it/pt for a million). @formatjs/intl-pluralrules@6.3.16 is correct (1 mismatch) but about 75 times slower per select on Hermes. It also throws on locales with no data loaded unless Intl.Locale is polyfilled too (about 96 KB gzipped in total). A 24-language shim built from make-plural (about 3 KB gzipped, no Intl dependency) gave 0 mismatches of 55,560 and correct i18next output, so that is the recommended approach. Assumption (3) holds even more strongly: DisplayNames is absent, not just unreliable, so language names must come from a static autonym table. Collator and localeCompare work and follow each language's sort rules. For money, Intl.NumberFormat currency output on Hermes/Apple matched V8 byte for byte for all 24 languages in my run. But on Apple it ignores signDisplay, compact notation, trailingZeroDisplay and roundingMode, rounds ties half-even (4.85→4.8, while V8 gives 4.9), and style:'unit' is broken (5 minutes prints as '300 seconds'). For dates, month and weekday names are safe on both platforms, with correct nominative/genitive forms on Apple ('listopad' alone vs '4 listopada'). formatRange is missing, and Apple differs from web in hour padding ('09:05'), uses U+202F before AM/PM, has a timeZoneName bug for en, and mislabels the part type for a standalone month. Assumption (5) only partly holds. On iOS, Intl's default locale is NSLocale.currentLocale, which follows the app bundle's declared localizations. Aura today declares none, so it always reports 'en-XX'. I verified in .app bundles on macOS that adding CFBundleLocalizations with the 24 codes makes the OS pick the best match from the user's ordered list ([uk,pl]→'pl-UA'). That makes item (8) a requirement for detection, not just metadata. On Android, AOSP source says the default locale is the OS best match against the APK's resource languages. The APK currently ships 86 of them through libraries (including uk and ru, but not ga or mt), so detection there needs localeFilters plus values-<lang> resources. This is from source only and still needs a device check in manor. Jest runs on Node with full ICU and will hide all of these gaps unless the test setup removes the missing APIs to imitate Hermes.

recommendations: Step 1 (plurals): add a 24-language Intl.PluralRules shim built on make-plural (pin 8.1.0), installed only `if (typeof Intl.PluralRules === 'undefined')`, as the very first import in index.js before i18next.init. The minimal-class version (prototype: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Volumes-Work-personal-ai-manors-aura-app-manor-project-slave-1/1d7b6620-d8b9-493c-a7cb-aeb6a03c6d67/scratchpad/hermes-intl/entries/mini24.js) is 3 KB gz, has no Intl dependency, and behaves identically on iOS, Android and Jest. It can be vendored as a generated file in shared/lib, matching the app's habit of baking data at authoring time. Do not use intl-pluralrules@2.0.1 as-is. Choose @formatjs only if all CLDR locales are needed, and then also add @formatjs/intl-locale and use polyfill-force.

Step 2 (tests): in jest.setup.js, imitate Hermes by deleting Intl.PluralRules, DisplayNames, RelativeTimeFormat, ListFormat, Locale and Segmenter, plus NumberFormat.prototype.formatToParts and DateTimeFormat.prototype.formatRange. Add a test comparing the shim with Node's native PluralRules for 0..2100 and the decimals 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 1.25, 10.1 across all 24 languages, the same matrix that gave 0/55,560 here. Add make-plural to transformIgnorePatterns.

Step 3 (i18next config): use supportedLngs = LANGUAGES, load: 'languageOnly' (or nonExplicitSupportedLngs), fallbackLng 'en', and keep cacheInBuiltFormats true. Do not use the relativetime or list formatters; write plural translation keys ('{{count}} days ago'). Either set react.useSuspense:false or load the active language's resources synchronously before the first render, for example with require()-based loaders, since Metro bundles every language anyway.

Step 4 (money): if web parity is wanted, format with a cached Intl.NumberFormat(lang, {style:'currency', currency:'USD'}).format(minor/100). It is safe on both platforms, and minor/100 is exact so rounding cannot diverge. For whole-dollar tiers, pass maximumFractionDigits:0 only when minor % 100 === 0. Never use formatToParts, signDisplay, notation, trailingZeroDisplay, roundingMode or style:'unit'. Pre-round ratings in JS before formatting.

Step 5 (dates): use cached Intl.DateTimeFormat(lang, {...}).format() for month, weekday and day names; standalone and in-date case forms come out right. Replace formatRange with two format() calls joined by an en dash. Avoid timeZoneName and don't rely on formatToParts part types for months. Keep the existing hand-built 24h formatClockTime unless the owner wants locale-specific clocks. Always pass the i18next language explicitly and never rely on the default locale.

Step 6 (language names): use a static autonym table in shared/config (24 entries such as 'Deutsch', 'Gaeilge', 'Malti', 'Ελληνικά', 'Български', 'Čeština'), sorted by a fixed order or Intl.Collator(currentLanguage). If the design shows the name in the UI language as well, put it in each language's namespace. Intl.DisplayNames is absent on both platforms.

Step 7 (device language, iOS): add CFBundleLocalizations with the 24 codes to Info.plist; this is required for detection, not just store metadata. Then take the language subtag of Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().locale, which the OS has already best-matched against the user's ordered list (verified: [uk,pl] → pl). If the full list is needed, Settings.get('AppleLanguages') provides it from RN core. A choice saved in Profile → Language overrides detection.

Step 8 (device language, Android): add androidResources.localeFilters with the 24 languages (AGP 8.12), a res/values-<lang>/strings.xml containing at least app_name for each language (especially ga and mt, which no library ships), and locales_config.xml / generateLocaleConfig for the Android 13 per-app language setting. Android's own best-match then picks among the 24, and Intl or I18nManager.localeIdentifier (underscore form) gives the result. Alternatively, extend the existing AuraDeviceCountry native module to return LocaleList.getDefault() as a full list.

Step 9 (manor verification after merge): on one iOS and one Android device, and ideally on the oldest supported OS (iOS 15.1, API 24), check Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Intl), that the shim is active, detection with system languages [uk, pl] and [ga, en], Android rounding of 4.85 to one decimal, and the hour/AM-PM output, so the Android source-only claims get confirmed.

findings.summary: Fonts are not a blocker for 21 of the 23 non-English targets. All 7 bundled faces cover every CLDR 48.2 main letter, upper and lower case, for cs da de es et fi fr ga hr hu it lt lv mt nl pl pt ro sk sl sv. Every character in aura-web's 976 translation files for those languages is also present, with one exception: Hanken Grotesk lacks U+202F (narrow no-break space). French uses it 24 times and as its Intl group separator, and it falls back to a system glyph invisibly. Greek and Bulgarian are not covered by either family. Bricolage has only π. Hanken has only Δ Ω μ π plus Greek punctuation (65 of 69 Greek exemplars missing in Hanken, 68 of 69 in Bricolage, all 60 Cyrillic missing in both). So el and bg fall back to a system font, and so do the "Ελληνικά"/"Български" rows in the Language sheet (design screen 15), which every user sees. I measured the fallback with CoreText on macOS 26.2, the same engine as iOS but not iOS itself: it is Helvetica / Helvetica-Bold. SemiBold and ExtraBold both collapse to Helvetica-Bold, and Hanken's μ/π and Bricolage's π splice into Greek words mid-word. From the AOSP and RN sources, Android also falls back per character, to the system sans-serif at each face's OS/2 weight, with the same splicing. Upstream: Bricolage has no Greek or Cyrillic anywhere. The Google Fonts build is identical to the bundled one and its repo has been dormant since 2023. Hanken's Google Fonts 'cyrillic-ext' subset contains only ₴. However, upstream marcologous/hanken-grotesk merged full modern Greek on 2026-09-02 (commit eff37d18). Google Fonts has not picked it up yet (#11159 is open), and there is still no Cyrillic. Those upstream statics are a drop-in replacement: same PostScript and family names, weights, vertical metrics and Latin advance widths. They are 73.6 KB each against 84–89 KB today. aura-web does nothing special: it loads the Google Fonts CSS API with a `system-ui` fallback, so the web already shows el/bg in the system font. Option (b), switching fonts per language through theme tokens, is structurally expensive. There are 207 fontFace() calls, and 91 files evaluate them inside module-level StyleSheet.create. Faces are therefore fixed at import time, so changing language would need a reload or a refactor. It also misses user-generated chat text, and needs about 290–790 KB for a 4-weight substitute. A better path is a build-time glyph merge: splice a donor family's Greek and Cyrillic into the 7 bundled files under the same PostScript names. I prototyped this with Commissioner as donor. It renders el/bg with zero fallback runs, keeps names and metrics, costs +143 KB raw (868 KB vs 726 KB) and needs no JS change. The prototype is not production-grade: it dropped GDEF and hinting. Golos and Onest, two of the suggested substitutes, are Cyrillic-only and cannot serve el. Commissioner, Manrope, Geologica and IBM Plex Sans have Greek, Cyrillic and Bulgarian locl; Inter has no Bulgarian locl. Against the first draft: it has no font step, which is a real gap. Item (6), the Language sheet, will show the gap to all users. Item (8)'s native list should add font coverage. Item (3), the static autonym table, is fine but needs these glyphs to render. Two related typography findings. RN iOS `textTransform: 'uppercase'` keeps Greek accents (tonos), which is wrong in Greek all-caps; Android drops them only when the device locale is Greek. Bulgarian letterforms (locl) never activate on iOS because RN sets no language attribute.

risks: The plan has no font step today. If it ships as is, el/bg (and the Ελληνικά/Български rows in the Language sheet, which every user sees) render in Helvetica (measured on macOS CoreText; iOS likely the same but unverified) or Roboto/OEM fonts. Greek words splice glyphs mid-word, and el/bg headlines drop from ExtraBold 800 to a plain Bold.

The iOS fallback family (Helvetica vs San Francisco) and the Android OEM fallback fonts are unverified. Only macOS CoreText and AOSP/RN source logic were examined, so expect device-specific looks until checked in manor.

The upstream Hanken Greek is a community contribution not yet reviewed by Google Fonts (#11159 open), and the static files are unhinted. Google Fonts QA may change glyphs later. Ω and µ advance widths differ from the bundled files, though the app does not use these characters today.

Per-language substitution through fontFace() (option b) does not take effect on a runtime language switch: 91 files evaluate fontFace() inside module-level StyleSheet.create. It also leaves user-generated chat text in fallback, needs per-family NATURAL_LINE/lineBoxLift values, and costs ~290–790 KB for a 4-weight substitute.

Native fallback chains are asymmetric. Android Typeface.CustomFallbackBuilder needs API 29 while the app's minSdk is 24, and the addCustomFont path re-applies weight 400 by default. iOS would need RN's RCTFont patched to add a cascade list.

A merged-font build is a type-production task. GDEF, hinting, kerning across scripts and stroke weight after x-height scaling need care, plus designer sign-off. A poor merge could look worse than clean system fallback.

The Latin-script languages have small traps. Romanian legacy cedilla ţ/Ţ falls back in Bricolage. French U+202F (used in web translations and in fr Intl output) is missing in Hanken. U+2010/U+2011/U+00AD/U+02BC are missing in both families. Each triggers per-glyph fallback.
Greek all-caps is wrong by default: RN iOS keeps tonos with textTransform 'uppercase', and Android drops them only under an el device locale. Around 20 uppercase eyebrow styles are affected.
Bulgarian letterforms differ by platform: never on iOS (RN sets no language attribute), on Android only when the device locale is bg.

The app and the web may diverge. aura-web gets Greek Hanken automatically when Google Fonts onboards #11159 (unpinned CSS API) but stays on system-ui for Bulgarian and Greek display. A merged app font would look different from the web unless the web self-hosts the same files.
recommendations: Step 1, write it into the plan: no font work is needed for the 21 Latin-script languages. Both families cover every CLDR main letter and every character the web translations use. Add an explicit font-coverage task for el and bg (and the Language sheet autonyms) to the first-draft plan's native/infra items (assumption 8).

Step 2, cheap and safe, can land before any strings: replace HankenGrotesk-{Regular,SemiBold,Bold}.ttf with the upstream marcologous/hanken-grotesk statics from fonts/ttf at commit eff37d18. Names, metrics and Latin widths are identical, it adds full Greek, saves 38,820 B and needs no JS change. Run fonts.test.ts, verify on iOS and Android in manor, and plan to re-sync when google/fonts #11159 lands (hinted, QA'd build).

Step 3, owner and designer decision for Bulgarian (both families) and Greek display (Bricolage). Preferred route, 3A: a reproducible fontTools build script, committed beside the fonts, that splices one donor family's Greek and Cyrillic into the 7 bundled files under the same PostScript names. That means zero JS or fonts.ts changes, coverage of UI strings, chat text and autonyms, identical behaviour on iOS and Android, and about +143 KB raw. Donor shortlist by measured fit: Commissioner (x-height .496 vs Hanken .493, weights 100–900, Greek+Cyrillic+BGR locl, ~42 KB per weight for Greek+Cyrillic); Manrope (smallest, ~23 KB per weight, but x-height .540 and 200–800 only); Geologica (x-height .495, wider). Production requirements: keep or merge GDEF, re-run ttfautohint (or accept unhinted), take the donor's π over Bricolage's so Greek words are uniform, add U+202F/U+2011 while at it, add the donor OFL, and extend fonts.test.ts with a generated coverage manifest for the 24 languages.

Step 3B, fallback if the owner accepts system fonts (parity with aura-web): ship el/bg on fallback, but still do Step 2 and optionally strip Bricolage's lone U+03C0 so Greek headlines fall back whole words instead of splicing. Accept the ExtraBold→Bold weight drop for el/bg headings.

Avoid option (b), per-language font tokens, and native fallback chains. The first is blocked by 91 module-level StyleSheets (restart or refactor needed), misses chat text and is the largest bundle cost. The second is Android API 29+ only, and iOS needs an RN patch.

Step 4: add translation lints to the i18n parity test. NFC-normalize all strings, which also turns U+037E/U+0387 into ; and ·. For ro, reject cedilla Ş ş Ţ ţ and require ș ț. Reject U+2010, U+2011, U+00AD and U+02BC, which neither font has. Allow French U+202F, or map it to U+00A0 unless the merged build adds the glyph.

Step 5, Greek all-caps: for el, do not rely on textTransform 'uppercase'. Add a pure shared/lib helper (NFD, drop U+0301 tonos, keep dialytika, add dialytika where a removed tonos split a diphthong, NFC), or have translators supply uppercase eyebrow strings. Check on device in manor whether Hermes' toLocaleUpperCase('el') already does this.

Step 6: only if the designer wants Bulgarian letterforms, bake them as default Cyrillic glyphs in the merged build, since bg is the only Cyrillic target. Otherwise accept default forms: RN will not trigger the BGR locl on iOS, and Android follows the device locale. Baking them would also restyle Russian/Ukrainian chat text.

Step 7, manor runtime checklist (slaves cannot run this): screenshots on an iOS simulator and an Android device of the Language sheet with all 24 autonyms, a Bricolage 800 headline in el and bg, Hanken 15/400 body in el and bg, an uppercase eyebrow in el, and a French price/percent containing U+202F. Compare against the current fallback (scratchpad/fonts-glyphs/out/compare.png).
Step 8: decide whether aura-web follows. If the app merges glyphs, the web either self-hosts the same merged WOFF2 files or knowingly stays on system-ui for bg and Greek display.

findings.summary: APP/src (443 production .ts/.tsx files, about 41k lines) holds about 628 user-visible copy strings counted per slice. That is about 554 distinct strings globally, roughly 2.5k English words, in 654 occurrences. 118 of them are template literals with interpolation and 55 distinct ones are accessibility labels. On top of that there are 245 English country names (+7 folded search keys), 69 hand-built weekday and month name entries in three separate tables, and 24 zodiac name and date-range strings. By slice, screens carry about 375 strings, features about 179, shared about 45 and entities about 29; the app layer has none. About 52% of copy is inline JSX in ui/ and about 30% already sits in 21 config files (7 of them named config/copy.ts), which map directly onto the web's `<slice>/config/locales/en.ts` pattern. The rest is about 10% in model hooks, 6% in lib and 2% in shared/api (Firebase auth error messages). First-draft assumptions this refutes or corrects: (a) there is no Redux or RTK Query anywhere (no redux in package.json or package-lock; stores are module-level with useSyncExternalStore and hold no copy). (b) profile-form has no zod and no validation messages; validation is boolean flags, and the messages live in create-account/edit-profile config. (c) The app already has a device-locale reader that tries I18nManager.getConstants().localeIdentifier before falling back to Intl (phone-auth/lib/device-country.ts:101-116). (d) Notifee channel names and texts exist and are drawn from a headless JS context (index.js:19-20). This confirms that i18n must bootstrap outside React. Structural hazards to fix before or during extraction: segment labels used as state and logic keys (Advisors, Horoscope Today/Tomorrow, Sessions Upcoming/Past, SegmentedControl renders the value as the label); a type literal used as copy (CheckoutVerb 'book' | 'start now' | 'extend' inside `Pay ${price} & ${verb}`); error messages resolved to strings inside the API layer (AuthError.message) and stored in state; module-level and memoised strings that would freeze the language. Formatting is all hand-made and English-only: three calendar tables with orders that disagree even in English (US 'Friday, August 14' versus UK 'Friday · 30 May'), '$' + toFixed money, '%' and decimal points. Node CLDR also shows that the design's day-plus-month-abbreviation blocks cannot be built from Intl for bg and lt (numeric months) or cs and fi. About 35 strings need plural rules; many sentences are built from fragments or put advisor and country names into slots that need grammatical case ('with {name}', "{name}'s", 'from {country}'). Much content is server-provided English shown verbatim: the advisor catalogue, horoscope, tarot, the session markers (with English-regex logic on them), season copy with English character limits, and 'Anonymous'. The BFF and http-client have no locale handling. The bundled fonts contain no Greek or Cyrillic glyphs, so el and bg will render in a system fallback font. The riskiest layout spots are the fixed-width DateStrip (58pt), the ticket stub (74pt), the absolutely positioned 'Biggest saving' tag, the fixed-height DailyCardBanner, one-line tickets and pay tiles, and the header, CTA-bar and footer rows. 64 of 159 test files (about 40%) assert English copy through react-test-renderer helpers. They will keep passing if i18next is initialised synchronously in jest.setup.js with the bundled en resources (passing `resources` makes init synchronous in i18next 26), useSuspense is false, keys resolve at render time, the English wording is unchanged and locale 'en' (not en-GB) is used for any Intl formatting.

Module-scope resolution (`export const X = t(...)`), the useMemo(…, []) date label, and error strings stored in state would freeze the first language. Tests will not catch this, because jest initialises English before any module loads.

AuthError messages are produced in shared/api (outside React), and push notifications are drawn by a headless JS task (index.js). Both need an i18n instance and the persisted language without the React tree. If the headless path is forgotten, notifications ship in English.

The calendar blocks (DateStrip, Sessions card, Reschedule) cannot be fed from Intl for bg/lt (numeric months) or cs/fi/hu (different order or numeric forms). Swapping the hand tables for Intl naively will produce '02 / 09' blocks; these languages need translated month-abbreviation tables or a redesign.

About 35 plural-sensitive strings and about 20 fragment-built sentences. Machine-style 1:1 extraction without restructuring will produce ungrammatical text in Slavic and Baltic languages and in fi, hu and el. Templates that put advisor and country names in case-governed slots ('with {name}', "{name}'s", 'from {country}') cannot be translated correctly without rewording.

Server-provided English (advisor catalogue, horoscope, tarot, session markers, season copy with English length budgets, review 'Anonymous', Console pushes) will sit next to translated chrome. The marker colour logic reads English text with a regex, so any server-side localisation of markers breaks it unless a machine-readable kind is added first.
Greek and Bulgarian will render in system fallback fonts (the bundled faces have no Greek or Cyrillic). The tight display line-heights (34/36) may also clip capital diacritics.

Fixed-geometry components (58pt DateStrip, 74pt ticket stub, the absolute 'Biggest saving' tag, the 148pt DailyCardBanner with overflow hidden, one-line tickets and tiles) will truncate or clip with typical +30–40% de/fi/hu/el expansion. No component uses adjustsFontSizeToFit.

Money stays USD with '$' + a decimal point, beside store-localised prices like '25,99 €'. A per-locale switch needs a decision on how USD is spelled (de '1,99 $', fr '1,99 $US', hu/pl/lt '1,99 USD', bg '1,99 щ.д.').
Translating OPENING_DRAFT, and users writing in their own language, changes what the advisor desk receives. This is an operations dependency (chatter language coverage) outside the app.
Policy numbers (24 h, 4 h, seven years, 25 MB, 6-digit) are written into prose in several strings. If they stay literal in 24 translations they will drift from the config values.
Tests run on Node's full ICU (78.2), so they cannot reveal Hermes Intl gaps. Using en-GB rather than 'en' for source formatting would break the 8 date-asserting and 22 money-asserting test files.
recommendations: Step 0 – structural fixes before any copy moves. (a) Give SEGMENTS, HOROSCOPE_DAYS and SESSION_SEGMENTS stable ids, change SegmentedControl to options {value,label}, and update filter-advisors.ts:32,36, use-home.ts:92 and SessionsScreen.tsx:48 to compare ids. (b) Split CheckoutVerb (use-checkout.ts:14) from its display text. (c) Make AuthError carry only `code`, with the screen mapping code to key, and make use-phone-auth/use-verify-otp store codes or keys rather than resolved strings. (d) Remove useMemo([]) for formatted labels, or add the language to the deps.

Step 1 – conventions, aligned with the web: `<slice>/config/locales/en.ts` per slice that has copy (about 31 slices plus shared). The 21 existing config copy/constants files convert almost mechanically. Never call t() at module scope: config exports keys or functions, and components and hooks call t at render. Give policy numbers (24 h, 4 h, 7 years, MAX_ATTACHMENT size, OTP length) interpolation parameters fed from config constants.

Step 2 – shared first, about 45 strings plus formatters. Create a 'common' namespace for repeated phrases keyed by meaning ('Go back', generic failure, 'Try again', 'Close', 'Check your connection…'), keeping the 'Review' and 'Today' homonyms as separate keys. Replace formatUsd/formatUsdMinor/formatUsdMinorCompact (42 call sites behind one module), percent and decimal formatting, formatFileSize and relativeDay with locale-aware versions. Keep formatClockTime as 24h for every language.

Step 3 – calendar: decide the English source style first (current code mixes US and UK). Then use per-language month-abbreviation and weekday resources for the block layouts (DateStrip, Sessions card, Reschedule, horoscope sign ranges), because CLDR gives numeric months for bg/lt and different orders for cs/fi/hu. Use Intl or a generated table for long dates, depending on what the Hermes investigation finds.

Step 4 – countries: reuse the authoring-time generator documented in countries.ts:27-28 to emit 24 tables from Node's full ICU (Intl.DisplayNames per language), each with locale collation order and diacritic-folded search keys. Keep all 245 names, because the unsupported-country message can name any of them. Reword 'We can't text numbers from {country} yet' so the name stands in the nominative, e.g. 'Country: {country} — we can't send codes there yet'.

Step 5 – rewrite rather than transliterate. Turn every fragment-concatenation site listed in the facts into one interpolated message, and use react-i18next <Trans> for the legal line with two links (PhoneAuthScreen.tsx:109-126) and for 'Sent to … · change'. Use i18next plurals (_one/_few/_many/_other) for the roughly 35 count strings, including the 'n min left' family and the StarPicker. Reword the name-in-case templates ('with {name}' → '{name} · reading', possessives → 'on the advisor's profile'), and replace the push body with a full gender-neutral sentence ('New message from your advisor').

Step 6 – then entities (about 29), features (about 179) and screens (about 375), one slice per task with all 24 languages, as the web rule does. Expect about 2.5k English words in total (about 57k words across 23 target languages) plus 245 generated country names per language.

Step 7 – layout pass with a pseudo-locale (+40% expansion and accented capitals) before real translations land. Fix DateStrip (allow 2 lines, or a short 'today' key with a length constraint), the ticket stub (adjustsFontSizeToFit or a 2-line stub), the 'Biggest saving' tag (constrain to the card width, allow 2 lines), DailyCardBanner (remove the fixed height or clamp lines), and the one-line CTAs and tiles (numberOfLines 2 or flexShrink). Add localized accessibilityLabels to the tab bar. Consider maxFontSizeMultiplier on fixed chips.

Step 8 – tests: in jest.setup.js, require the en.ts locale files directly (not slice index files, mirroring the web's 'Direct imports, not the public APIs' note in vitest.setup.ts) and call i18next.use(initReactI18next).init({ lng:'en', fallbackLng:'en', resources:{ en }, react:{ useSuspense:false }, interpolation:{ escapeValue:false } }) synchronously. Keep English wording byte-identical during extraction so the 64 English-asserting test files stay green. Add a completeness test like the web's i18n.test.ts (missing keys, blank strings, dropped {{placeholders}}) and a test or lint check that forbids module-scope t().

Step 9 – non-React entry points: a tiny `getI18n()` bootstrap usable from index.js (headless FCM / Notifee) and from shared/api, which reads the persisted language file (Documents, not Caches) before displayMessageNotification. Re-create the Notifee channels with localized names on language change; createChannel already runs on every display.

Step 10 – server-text boundary: add client-side overrides where the client can (render a localized 'Anonymous' when review.anonymous is true; ask the BFF for a machine-readable marker kind before anyone localizes markers). Treat the advisor catalogue, horoscope, tarot texts, season copy and Console pushes as English-only in v1 unless the owner decides otherwise, and say so in the plan. Season copy would need per-locale fields plus per-locale length limits in contracts.

Step 11 – fonts: decide between shipping Greek- and Cyrillic-capable builds of Bricolage/Hanken (whether such builds exist was not checked) and accepting system fallback for el/bg, and check visually.

Step 12 – after extraction, add an ESLint rule against raw JSX text and literal user-facing strings (e.g. an i18next no-literal-string style rule; availability and version not checked) so the about 550 extracted strings do not come back as hard-coded literals.

Clean up while touching copy: delete or gate the 'Visa ···· 4242' / 'Change' stub row (TopUpSheet.tsx:103,109); derive APP_VERSION_LABEL from the build instead of the stale '1.0.0'; normalise English typography ('Sending...' versus '…', straight versus curly apostrophes, 'Top Up' versus 'Top up') before translators copy the inconsistencies.
open_questions_for_owner: Can the advisor desk (chatters) work in all 24 languages? If not, should the OPENING_DRAFT prefill and the advisor greeting stay English, and should users be told chats are in English?

Server content: should advisor bios/roles/specialties/greetings, horoscope texts, tarot names/keywords/meanings, session markers and season campaign copy be localised server-side (Accept-Language plus per-locale fields), or stay English in the first i18n release?
Which English is the source: US ('Friday, August 14', 'Jun 02') or UK ('Friday 14 August', '30 May')? The current code mixes both.

The calendar blocks show a day number over a month abbreviation. For bg/lt/cs/fi CLDR has no usable short month for this; should translators supply abbreviations, or should those locales get a different block design?
Is system-font fallback acceptable for Greek and Bulgarian, or should Greek- and Cyrillic-capable fonts be licensed and bundled?
Legal pages exist only in English (aura-app.cc/terms, /privacy; localized paths 404). Are English-only Terms and Privacy acceptable for EU locales, or must they be translated before launch?
Should USD amounts be spelled per locale ('1,99 $', '1,99 $US', '1,99 USD'), or keep '$1.99' everywhere to match the dollar-denominated balance?
Should brand and marketing lines be translated ('PSYCHIC · TAROT · DREAMS', 'STEP 2 OF 2', '50% OFF First Session', 'CODE'/'SALE' stubs), or kept in English as brand voice?
Should Firebase Console announcement campaigns be targeted by language? They are drawn verbatim by the app.
Should the country picker sort and search by localized names? That needs 24 generated tables of 245 names.
Should the birth-date mask follow locale order (year-first for hu/lt/sv), or stay DD.MM.YYYY for every language?

findings.summary:
aura-web's i18n is small and has barely changed: i18next 26.5.3 + react-i18next 17.1.0, four files in shared/i18n plus shared/config/languages.ts, touched in only three commits. All visible copy is split into 39 namespaces, one per slice. The design is worth copying as types and conventions, but its runtime cannot be lifted into the app unchanged.

CONFIRMED (first-draft assumption 1, partly): the LANGUAGES list (en + 23 EU), the Translation<typeof en> type with plural support, and one config/locales/ folder per slice with ResourceNamespaceMap for typed t(). I checked the type with tsc in a scratch project. A missing key, an extra key, a missing nested key, a misspelt plural category or a missing language all fail to compile. A Polish file with no _few/_many forms, or a translation that drops {{name}}, still compiles; only the web's i18n.test.ts catches those.

REFUTED (the 'lazy per-language loaders' part of assumption 1): Metro's asyncRequire serves import() from the same bundle, so splitting by language saves nothing. Worse, the app's own Babel config leaves import() untransformed under test, and Jest 29.7.0 throws 'A dynamic import callback was invoked without --experimental-vm-modules' (reproduced in scratch). The app should use synchronous require loaders and keep the Record<TranslatedLanguage,…> type that enforces a file for every language.

Plurals (assumption 2, from my side): when Intl.PluralRules is missing, i18next 26 quietly falls back to one/other for plain codes such as 'pl' and logs nothing (checked in the i18next source). The web test takes the expected forms from Node's ICU (CLDR 48, so es/fr/it/pt need _many, ga/mt need five forms). On the app the test must use the same plural data as the runtime polyfill.

Names and formats (assumption 3): the web relies on Intl.DisplayNames for language and country names, plus Intl Collator, NumberFormat and DateTimeFormat (including formatRange and formatToParts), always in the UI language. The app already avoids DisplayNames and Intl time formatting on Hermes. Static tables generated ahead of time are small: about 5 KB for language names and about 78 KB for country names across 24 languages. Someone also has to decide between the app's 24-hour clock and '$1.99' and the web's per-language output ('06:30 PM' in English, '1,99 $US' in French).

Size: 751 English strings (41 plural bases, so about 710 messages), average 27.8 characters, median 20. That is 975 files and 1.21 MB of TS source. All 24 languages compile to 986 KB of Hermes bytecode (325 KB gzipped) with the local hermesc. The app's own copy is about 61% of the web's by characters, which suggests about +0.6 MB on today's 3.47 MB bundle.

Reuse: only 8 of 37 slices match in both layer and name. Identical-copy overlap ranges from 83% (daily/tarot) and 70% (write-review, profile, auth) down to 17–22% (booking, payment, chat) and 14% (home). Overall, 241 of the app's 523 non-date strings (46%) exactly match a web English string, so their 23 translations can be copied over.

Shared translations package: not worth it now. AURAD-0019 (owner-ratified) shares only @aura/contracts. Each slice owns its strings, the flows differ (store purchase vs web payment, tap vs hover, device vs browser), and the two clients ship on different schedules. A shared package would turn every copy fix into a change across three repos. Copy-and-adapt plus a one-off translation harvest with source links is the better option.

History: on 2026-10-20 the owner reversed 'no i18n' («добавь так же переводы через i18 и запиши правило про добавления переводов в каждой задаче») and set the languages («en, и все страны EC»). The agents wrote the translations themselves, later as 3–4 parallel agents per language group. Native-speaker review is still open (bg, el, mt first).

Language picker (assumption 6): the owner replaced the 24-row radio list with an autocomplete («в списке языков хорошо бы сделать селектор автокомплит»). The choice is kept per browser, not on the account. App design screen 15 is still a 6-language radio list with a 'Choose' button.

Assumption 8, Firebase part: confirmed, the web sets firebaseAuth.languageCode before sending the SMS.

Assumption 9 (send Accept-Language): refuted as useful today. Neither the web nor the BFF uses it; server texts stay in English by owner decision, and session markers are matched by their exact English wording.

Problems the web ran into: the namespace list is kept in two places that must match (app/config/i18n.ts and vitest.setup.ts), and both files kept conflicting when parallel branches merged. Advisor names don't decline correctly in Slavic, Baltic and Finnic languages. Translations run up to 1.74× longer than English (Irish). Translated accessibility labels needed an extra WCAG test. And the i18n test does not check the <tag> markup used by <Trans>.

facts.claim: Type mechanics: Translation<Source> = Plain<Source> & Plurals<Source>. Plain mirrors every non-plural key (recursively) as string; Plurals requires <base>_other and allows optional _zero/_one/_two/_few/_many for each English plural base. I18nNamespace<Source> = { name, source, load: Readonly<Record<TranslatedLanguage, () => Promise<{default: Translation<Source>}>>> }. Each <lang>.ts is `export default {...} satisfies Translation<typeof en>`; each locales/index.ts augments i18next's ResourceNamespaceMap (the i18next 26 per-package namespace map) so t() keys are typed per namespace; CustomTypeOptions is not augmented.
facts.evidence: WEB/src/shared/i18n/namespace.ts:4-47; WEB/src/pages/me/config/locales/index.ts:5-40, pl.ts:1-84; WEB/node_modules/i18next/typescript/options.d.ts:30-54 (ResourceNamespaceMap doc); grep CustomTypeOptions in WEB/src -> none

facts.claim: Compile-time guarantees, checked with tsc 5.9.3 against a copy of namespace.ts: these fail to compile — missing key (TS1360), extra key (TS2353), missing nested key (TS2322), misspelt plural suffix e.g. reviews_fewx (TS2561), language missing from the loader table (TS2740). These still compile: Polish without _few/_many, and a translation that dropped {{name}}. Only the i18n test catches those two.
Plural support was missing from the first version of Translation (it forced an exact mirror of the English keys) and was added one task later in AURAT-0103 (commit aefc5db).

Runtime: initI18n registers a custom BackendModule. English is bundled through resources.en with partialBundledLanguages:true; other languages come from each namespace's loader; unknown namespaces resolve to {}; a loader error goes to the i18next callback, which then falls back to English. Options: lng, fallbackLng 'en', supportedLngs LANGUAGES, load 'languageOnly', ns = every namespace, defaultNS false, interpolation.escapeValue false, returnNull false, react.useSuspense false. A languageChanged listener sets document.documentElement.lang.
Startup: main.tsx awaits initI18n(I18N_NAMESPACES, startLanguage()) before createRoot().render, so the first render is already in the visitor's language.

Language choice: startLanguage() = rememberedLanguage() ?? detectLanguage(). rememberedLanguage reads localStorage 'aura.language' inside try/catch and checks it against LANGUAGES; detectLanguage takes navigator.languages, lowercases each, keeps the base code (de-AT -> de) and returns the first one shipped, else 'en'. chooseLanguage writes localStorage, then awaits i18next.changeLanguage, so the old language stays on screen until the new strings load. The choice is per browser; the comment says 'the profile has no language field'.

Display names come from Intl: languageName() uses Intl.DisplayNames([inLanguage],{type:'language'}) plus toLocaleUpperCase and falls back to the code in upper case. The sign-in country list uses Intl.DisplayNames region names in the UI language and sorts with Intl.Collator.

Picker implementation: pages/me LanguagePicker renders the shared Combobox (ARIA APG list autocomplete). Each option shows the language's own name as the label, its name in the current UI language as a grey hint, its English name as a search keyword, and a lang attribute. The current value is LANGUAGES.find(l => l === i18n.resolvedLanguage). Picking calls chooseLanguage, which switches immediately. Search ignores case and accents via normalize('NFD') + /\p{Diacritic}/gu.

Picker history and owner decisions: the spec called for 24 languages under their own names (Intl.DisplayNames, 'переводить нечего'), a check mark on the current one, the choice kept in localStorage and 'На сервер не уходит (поля нет)'. Owner approval: «Язык — да, 24 языка» / «Выбор языка — делаем, 24 языка, в браузере». It shipped as a 24-row radiogroup. The owner then asked «в списке языков хорошо бы сделать селектор автокомплит», which produced the Combobox; next «да, выноси в shared», which moved it to shared/ui/combobox. Steiger flagged a separate features/choose-language slice as insignificant (one consumer), so the list lives in pages/me. Steiger caps shared/lib at 15 modules, so the search helper went to shared/model.

The i18n test (Vitest) loops over every namespace. It checks that (a) English has its own plural forms per Intl.PluralRules('en'). For each of the 23 languages it checks: (b) the same plain keys as English; (c) plural forms exactly equal to new Intl.PluralRules(lang).resolvedOptions().pluralCategories; (d) no blank string; (e) the same {{placeholders}} as English, where plural forms are compared with <base>_other and may drop {{count}}. A final test checks that vitest.setup's namespace list equals I18N_NAMESPACES. It checks neither the <tag> markup used by <Trans> nor translations left identical to English.

One slice has its own locale test, an owner-requested WCAG 2.5.3 guard: in all 24 languages, the screen-reader name of 'Book session' must start with its visible label. Eight translations (da de es it nl pt ro sv) had to be reworded for it.

The namespace list exists twice: app/config/i18n.ts (I18N_NAMESPACES, imported through each slice's public API) and vitest.setup.ts (direct imports, because loading @/shared in setup loaded api modules before vi.mock could replace them). An eslint override turns off no-restricted-imports for vitest.setup.ts. Both files caused merge conflicts between parallel slots in practice.

recommendations: Step 1, copy rather than share. Port with '// Ported from aura-web <path> (<ID>)' headers: shared/config/languages.ts (drop LANGUAGE_STORAGE_KEY), shared/i18n/namespace.ts verbatim (the plural-aware version), detect-language (fed the device's ordered list of preferred languages, not a single locale), the language-choice shape (stored choice, else device language; choosing = persist + changeLanguage), and the <slice>/config/locales/{en.ts,<lang>.ts,index.ts} layout with ResourceNamespaceMap.

Step 2, change the loaders. Use synchronous ones, `load: { de: () => require('./de').default, … }`, typed `() => Translation<Source>`, and keep the Readonly<Record<TranslatedLanguage, Loader>> type so a missing language still fails to compile. Start i18next synchronously (initAsync:false, en plus the start language as resources). The only thing to await before first render is reading the stored choice, which can happen during the existing splash screen.

Step 3, keep one namespace registry. Make it a single file that imports only locale modules (<slice>/config/locales, plain data with no api imports), used by both the app's i18n init and jest.setup.js, with an eslint exception for that one file (or generate it with a script). This avoids the web's conflicts between two lists and its vi.mock ordering problem.

Step 4, port i18n.test.ts to Jest (describe.each/test.each exist there) and strengthen it. Take plural categories from the same plural data the runtime polyfill uses, not Node ICU. Add a check that <tag> markup is preserved in <Trans> strings. Add a report of translations left identical to English, with an allowlist (Aura, Apple Pay, Google Play, OK, Tarot…). Add a startup or unit check that Intl.PluralRules('pl') reports few/many after the polyfill loads.

Step 5, clean up the English before extracting a slice. Turn fragment strings into whole-sentence keys (the legal line via <Trans> with <Text onPress> links; separate keys for the 'saved with offer' and 'saved with campaign {{label}}' variants). Change helpers that return English text (relativeDay, refusal-copy, phase-copy, block-discount) to return data kinds and let screens pick the keys, as the web's dates.ts RelativeDay does. Map server error codes to closed unions before calling t(), like the web's refusal.ts.

Step 6, harvest the web's translations. Write a one-off script: for each new app en.ts value that exactly matches a web en.ts value (about 241 strings, 46%), copy the 23 translations from the web file and record the source (web namespace:key) so a reviewer can trace it. Translate only the remaining ~280 strings, and reuse the web's per-language register and terms (informal de/es/nl/sv/da/fi/et/hu/ro…, formal bg/cs/el/fr/hr/lt/lv/pt/sk/sl) so both clients sound the same.

Step 7, generate name tables ahead of time, the way countries.ts was made. Build them with Node ICU: language autonyms plus names in every UI language (576 entries, about 5 KB) and country names per UI language (about 78 KB), with pre-folded search keys. Don't call Intl.DisplayNames or String.normalize at runtime.

Step 8, pin down the formatting policy before migrating formatters. Either adopt per-language Intl formats like the web (once Hermes output is verified on both platforms) or keep the 24-hour/'$1.99' hand formatting with translated month and weekday tables. Either way, give every lib formatter an explicit `language` parameter, as the web's shared/lib does.

Step 9, bring back Profile → Language as a BottomSheet with a search field over 24 rows (own name, name in the current UI language, English name as keyword). Reuse the CountryPickerSheet pattern (memoized rows, FlatList, pre-folded keys); that also matches the owner's web request for autocomplete. Get the owner to choose between switching instantly (web) and committing with a 'Choose' button (design 15).

Step 10, set the RN Firebase auth language from i18n.language before sending the OTP, as the web does with languageCode. Initialize i18n on the index.js path so the headless push handlers and the Alert texts are localized too.

Step 11, keep server-owned content in English and say so explicitly in the specs, as the web did. Translate the two session markers by exact match. Don't spend effort on Accept-Language now: the BFF ignores it. Put the machine-readable marker and a contract-level language field (AURAF-0020-053) in the backlog.

Step 12, process. Extract slice by slice with all 24 languages in each task, and adopt the web's rule 9 once extraction is complete. Because the app is a retrofit, add a lint guard (e.g. no-restricted-syntax on JSXText containing letters in ui/, plus literal string props like accessibilityLabel/placeholder/title). Keep an owner-approved English-only exception for dev tooling. Put common phrases (Try again, Go back, Close, OK, Cancel, Done) in the shared namespace from the start so keys don't have to move later.

Step 13, quality. Schedule native-speaker review for bg, el, mt and ga first, and before a store release for store-facing and push texts. Lay out every screen with the longest languages (ga, el, de, fr, mt). Translate accessibilityLabel strings and keep the web's WCAG 2.5.3 'label in name' test for them.

Step 14, no shared translations package now. Revisit when server-side localization is scheduled; at that point move the LANGUAGES/Language code set into @aura/contracts so the BFF and both clients agree on codes, while each client keeps its own translations.

findings.summary: The BFF (aura-bff develop @ c8d78cf) and @aura/contracts v0.27.0 have no concept of language at all. Nothing reads Accept-Language or a locale. There is no language column on User or DeviceToken and no language field on the profile. Every piece of server-authored content is single-language English. Pushes are already language-neutral on the wire: the only FCM send is a data-only {type:'message.new', advisorId}, and the device draws the text itself (title = persona name, body and channel names = app constants). So localizing push is client-only work, including starting i18n inside the headless JS context. The one exception is Firebase Console campaigns: the operator types that text, and it needs per-language targeting. Errors need no server work either: the app lifts only status and `code`, never ApiError.message, and promo refusals are worded by code. If only the client is localized, the following stay English: the advisor catalog (role, tagline, bio, specialties and the greeting bubble), the 78-card tarot deck (name, keywords, daily; also embedded in client sentences like "You chose {name}" and "I drew {name} today…"), the two session markers (thread and chats preview), seasonal hero and ticket copy, the campaign discount label, the server's literal 'Anonymous', the fallback captions of spreads and invites, the legal pages, the OTP SMS and whatever the chatters type. That is exactly the state the web shipped in by owner decision (season copy kept English with lang="en", card texts shown as-is, markers translated by exact match), so a zero-server baseline gives parity. First-draft assumption (8) is CONFIRMED and sharpened: the app never calls setLanguageCode. It must call auth().setLanguageCode(<chosen>) right before verifyPhoneNumber, as the web does. RNFB v24's modular useDeviceLanguage throws. setLanguageCode(null) means useAppLanguage, which is the device's language, not the in-app choice. Assumption (9), "send Accept-Language", is REFUTED in its naive form. The BFF ignores it today. RN on iOS already sends an implicit Accept-Language taken from the device's first language: a CFNetwork probe sent "de-DE,de;q=0.9" for a German-first process with only an `en` bundle. Android sends none, and browsers send their own preferences. A BFF that honoured Accept-Language would therefore localize content for old English-only iOS builds, and for web users whose in-app choice differs. Use an explicit signal that only new clients send: a `lang` query parameter appended in each client's single HTTP function. This is harmless today because every query schema and RegisterDeviceRequest is non-strict. The minimum coherent server/contract work is small and additive. In contracts: a shared LANGUAGES list, an optional machine-readable `Message.marker`, and an optional `language` on the profile. In the BFF: a language resolver, `users.language`, the marker kind derived in toDto (no migration), and a `client_language` desk attribute so chatters know which language to answer in. Ordering trap: ProfilePatchRequest is `.strict()`, so the BFF must be deployed before any client sends `language`, or Create Account / Edit Profile get a 400. Never localize marker *content* on the server: the app's tone regex and the web's exact match both parse the English text. Add a kind instead. The heavy part is content. For the tarot deck the owner already chose server-side translations (AURAT-0137-006 §3A, backlog AURAF-0020-053); that is ≈9.9k chars × 23 languages. Advisor personas are ≈9.0k chars, the bios owner-supplied and kept "verbatim"; translating them implies chatters answer in the user's language (BFF TECH-DEBT #37). Seasonal copy is entered as "Тексты — en", its limits are measured for English at 316pt, and app-config is public with max-age=60, no Vary, and is also cached to a file. Two features not built yet must be language-aware from day one: the horoscope (route missing, 404 → section hidden) and BFF email sign-in (AURAT-0131 via Resend). Storing the language server-side requires a privacy-policy line, since today's policy lists only token, platform, time zone and IP. Recommended order: (1) owner decisions; (2) app-only pieces; (3) contracts v0.28.0; (4) the minimal BFF work, deployed; (5) clients start PATCHing `language` and render the marker kind; (6) tarot translations; (7) advisor translations if the chat-language policy allows; (8) seasonal copy per language. Per-device language, two-way chat translation, an advisor language filter and translated legal pages can wait.

findings.summary:
Scope: APP = /Volumes/Work/personal/ai-manors/aura-app-manor/project/slave-1/master (develop @ 28633b4). Evidence comes from the app's own Hermes build (250829098.0.10, the macOS slice of the iOS pod, run in throwaway app bundles), Foundation/CF and AOSP sources, javap on the AARs the build resolves, and the app's build outputs. Nothing was run on an iOS or Android device.

(1) Draft item 5, detecting the language with Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().locale, is REFUTED for today's iOS build. Hermes takes [NSLocale currentLocale]. Foundation matches that locale's language against the app's localizations. Aura declares only 'en' (no CFBundleLocalizations, no .lproj files, knownRegions en/Base). So Intl returns 'en-<region>' for every user, e.g. 'en-DE' for a German user. UIKit-provided strings are English for the same reason (RN Alert's default OK/Cancel, SFSafariViewController, the pickers). Once en plus the 23 EU codes are declared, the same call returns the best supported language over the user's whole preference list: [ru-ES, es-ES] gives es-ES, [ga-IE, en-IE] gives ga-IE, pt-BR gives pt-BR. That value equals Bundle.main.preferredLocalizations[0], so iOS needs no native module for detection.

(2) On Android, Intl and Locale.getDefault() return the resource-negotiated locale. Today's APK carries 87 library locale folders (ru, uk, ar…) and none for ga or mt, so a [ru, es] user would get 'ru'. Restrict the APK's locales with androidResources.localeFilters, and read the per-app and system lists from a small native module.

(3) Draft items 2 and 3 are CONFIRMED. This Hermes has no Intl.PluralRules, DisplayNames, RelativeTimeFormat, ListFormat or Locale on either platform.

(4) Draft item 8 is CONFIRMED, with corrections:
- iOS needs InfoPlist strings, best as a String Catalog that compiles to <lang>.lproj/InfoPlist.strings (verified with xcstringstool). It also needs CFBundleLocalizations and knownRegions.
- Android needs a hand-written locales_config.xml. AGP's generateLocaleConfig would list the ~87 library locales and leave out ga and mt.
- Android needs AppLocalesMetadataHolderService with autoStoreLocales.
- MainActivity needs locale|layoutDirection in configChanges. Without it, a language change recreates the activity and RN remounts the whole tree, losing navigation because none is persisted.

(5) Draft item 4, a react-native-fs file, is REFINED per platform:
- Android: the OS per-app locale should be the single store. AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales writes it to LocaleManager on 13+ and to AppCompat's file on 12 and below, and AppCompat migrates it automatically when the device upgrades to 13. It stays in sync with Settings → Apps → Language, keyboards and native resources. Only headless starts on API 32 and below need a tiny mirror.
- iOS: there is no supported API to set the app's language (Apple DTS: AppleLanguages is not API). The Settings Language row is hidden unless the user has 2 or more preferred languages, and iOS kills and relaunches the app when the language changes. So the in-app sheet keeps a small override file (in Documents, not Caches), reconciled against the OS language on a newest-change-wins rule.

(6) react-native-localize 3.7.2 (TurboModule, maintained) is not worth adding. It lacks the Android setter we need, and Intl is enough on iOS.

(7) Native side effects to wire:
- Notifee channel names must be re-created when the language changes (Android docs prescribe this).
- The BFF's FCM pings are data-only and rendered in a headless JS context, so language resolution must work without React or an Activity.
- Firebase SMS needs auth().setLanguageCode(lang) before verifyPhoneNumber; useDeviceLanguage throws in RNFB 24.

- getAppLocales(): API ≥33 → getSystemService(LocaleManager).applicationLocales.toLanguageTags(). Below 33 → AppCompatDelegate.getApplicationLocales().toLanguageTags(), or a SharedPreferences mirror when that is empty (cold headless start).
- getSystemLocales(): API ≥33 → LocaleManager.systemLocales; else Resources.getSystem().configuration.locales.toLanguageTags().
- setAppLocales(tags): inside UiThreadUtil.runOnUiThread, call AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags(tags)), and write the mirror below 33. '' means follow the system.
- openAppLocaleSettings(): API ≥33 → Intent(Settings.ACTION_APP_LOCALE_SETTINGS, Uri.fromParts("package", packageName, null)) with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK; else fall back to Linking.openSettings().

STEP 4 — JS language resolution, platform files behind one async resolveStartLanguage(): Promise<Language> (e.g. src/shared/i18n/device-language.android.ts and .ios.ts; the repo already uses .android.ts platform files).
- Android: base code of appLocales[0] if it is in LANGUAGES; else detectLanguage(systemLocales), a port of the web's detect-language.ts; else 'en'.
- iOS: os = detectLanguage([Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().locale]); this is already the best match once STEP 1 lands. Read the override from `${DocumentDirectoryPath}/app-language.json` = {language, osLanguage}, using the write-aside-then-move pattern of config-cache.ts but NOT CachesDirectoryPath. If a record exists and record.osLanguage === os, use record.language. Otherwise delete the record and use os, so the newest change wins after a Settings or device-language change (iOS relaunches the app on those).
- Await this before the first render (the splash is already async) and in index.js's headless handlers before any t() call.
- First launch: prompt nothing, persist nothing, and never pin the detected language natively, so device language changes keep flowing through.

STEP 5 — Choosing in the sheet (Profile → Languages, design 15).
- Android: await AuraAppLocale.setAppLocales(lang), then i18n.changeLanguage(lang). With configChanges there is no recreation or remount, and Settings → Apps → Aura → Language, the keyboard (IMEs read LocaleManager) and TalkBack strings follow.
- iOS: i18n.changeLanguage(lang), then save {language: lang, osLanguage: os}, or delete the record when lang === os. Optionally show a secondary 'Change in iOS Settings' action → Linking.openSettings() for prompts and system UI.
- If the owner agrees, add a 'Device language' row: setAppLocales('') on Android, delete the record on iOS.
- Android only: on AppState 'active', resolve again (catches a change made in Settings while backgrounded, and system language changes) and call changeLanguage if it differs. iOS needs no listener.

STEP 6 — Native side effects of the current language. Subscribe once to i18n 'languageChanged' and also run at startup.
(a) Android: create both Notifee channels with translated names. Add ensureMessagesChannel next to ensureAnnouncementsChannel in features/push. MESSAGES_CHANNEL_NAME, ANNOUNCEMENTS_CHANNEL_NAME, MESSAGE_NOTIFICATION_BODY and MESSAGE_NOTIFICATION_FALLBACK_TITLE become translated strings, read after the headless i18n init.
(b) Firebase: call auth().setLanguageCode(i18n.language) right before auth().verifyPhoneNumber in shared/api/firebase/auth.service.ts. Use an explicit code, not null, so the in-app override wins.
(c) Send Accept-Language: <lang> in shared/api/bff/http-client.ts:60 and upload.ts:79.
(d) shared/lib/open-url.ts: add headers: {'Accept-Language': lang} to the Android options. SFSafariViewController cannot set headers, so localize legal URLs by path or query if the web supports it.
(e) Always pass translated button texts to Alert.alert.
(f) When formatters move to Intl, pass the locale explicitly (`${lang}-${region}`, region from the system locale) and never rely on Intl's default.

STEP 8 — Ops (owner): add App Store Connect and Play Console listing plus IAP display-name localizations for the languages each console supports. After the first build with lproj, check the App Store 'Languages' line. Check Firebase SMS template coverage for ga and mt.

STEP 9 — Device matrix in manor before merge (slaves cannot run devices).
- iOS, device in de: app in de; camera prompt in de; Settings → Aura → Language visible (with 2 preferred languages, or with UIPrefersShowingLanguageSettings on 1); changing it relaunches in the new language; an in-app override survives a restart and is dropped after an OS change.
- Android 14: the sheet updates Settings → Apps → Language and vice versa; a Settings change while backgrounded is applied on resume without remounting.
- Android 12: the choice survives restart, and a notification for a killed app arrives in the chosen language.
- TalkBack role names in the chosen language; Custom Tab receives Accept-Language; channel names update in system settings; OTP SMS arrives in the chosen language.

ALTERNATIVE (minimum native code, if the panel rejects Kotlin): skip the module, AppCompat and localeConfig on Android. Use the same JS override file and reconcile rule on both platforms, with os = Intl's language subtag. The price:
- Android Settings is not in sync, and keyboards and TalkBack follow the system language.

findings.summary: The design handoff has exactly one way to change the language: Profile → 'Languages' row (globe icon, value 'English') opens the 'Choose language' bottom sheet. The sheet has a close ✕, a subtitle, a radio list (the selected row gets a coral filled circle with a white check) and a primary 'Choose' button that commits the choice (WORKSPACE/.claude/design_handoff_aura/README.md:119,219,298; prototype/settings-chat.jsx:8,196-218; screens 14 and 15). There is no language step at first run. The flow is Splash → Wizard → Phone → SMS → App (ONBOARDING.md:18-22). The prototype's onboarding screens get only onDone/onNext/onBack callbacks, and only the Settings row calls nav.sheet('lang') (app.jsx:98,252-255,291). So the subtitle 'You can change this later in your profile.' contradicts the sheet's only entry point; it is not evidence of a first-run prompt. First-draft assumption 6 (bring back the row and the sheet) is CONFIRMED, with fixes. use-profile.ts:66-69 hides every sheet row while billing is off, so the Language row would vanish. ProfileMenu has no slot for a value and keys rows by their label. The old AURAF-0001 LanguageSheet (removed in 1f65d57) can be restored as a starting point, but it was written before face-based fonts and before swipe-to-close (dragFromGrip). The design's 300pt list holds 6 placeholder languages, including es-419/pt-BR variants that are out of scope. With 24 rows it needs a bounded scroll of about 55-60% of the window (the web uses 62% on phones), dragFromGrip, a visible scroll indicator and an initial scroll to the selected row. On parity with the web: rows show the autonym with the name in the current UI language as a grey hint. The choice is per browser (localStorage 'aura.language'), never sent to the server, applies instantly, and can only be made after sign-in. The owner had the web's 24-row radio list replaced with an autocomplete field (AURAT-0136-009). Recommended app model, in order: (a) one per-device preference, 'device' (the default) or an explicit language. Detection takes the first supported language from the device's ordered list, as the web does. This refines assumption 5: on iOS, RN 0.85.3's I18nManager exports no localeIdentifier, and on Android it exports only the first locale. (b) The sheet keeps the design's pick-then-'Choose' (safe against mis-taps in a long list). It shows autonym plus hint, ordered 'Device language' → English → the other 23 by autonym. (c) The language is applied after the sheet's onClosed and the screens re-render in place, without remounting navigation. (d) The row value shows the autonym of the language in effect. (e) No first-launch prompt. Two findings were not in the first draft. First, neither bundled font has Greek or basic Cyrillic glyphs, so bg, el and even the autonyms Български and Ελληνικά fall back to system fonts (the web falls back the same way). Second, server-written content (advisor role/bio/greeting, season copy, session markers) stays in English, so the screens mix languages. On assumption 7: shipping detection before every string is extracted would push a half-translated app to every non-English phone, so the runtime language must stay English behind a flag until coverage is complete. Accessibility: use role 'radio' with accessibilityState.checked, not selected. With checked, iOS reads 'radio button, checked/unchecked' and Android exposes a checkable RadioButton. Put accessibilityLanguage on the autonym rows (iOS only).

risks: Rollout: if device-language detection goes live while strings are still being extracted layer by layer (assumption 7), every user whose phone is set to an EU language automatically gets a half-translated app, release after release. The app ships builds often (versionCode 36 / 1.0.11).
The Language row disappears whenever billing is off if it is added as a 'sheet' row, because use-profile.ts:66-69 filters out every sheet row while walletEnabled is false.

In-place language switching misses strings captured at module scope: PROFILE_MENU_ROWS labels (PROMO_CODES_LABEL), the splash TAGLINE, notification constants, the BottomSheet scrim's 'Close'. These stay in the old language until the app restarts, unless they become keys resolved at render time.

Remounting the navigation tree on a language change (for example key={language}) would reset every tab stack (open chat, scroll positions). Doing it while the language Modal is presented risks the iOS two-modal deadlock or invisible-layer bug (AURAT-0020).

iOS detection may always return English. RN 0.85.3's I18nManager has no localeIdentifier on iOS, and Hermes' Intl default locale may resolve to the bundle's only localization ('en') unless CFBundleLocalizations is declared or AppleLanguages is read. The Hermes part is unverified.

Android exposes only the first locale, so a user whose phone lists [uk, pl] gets English in the app but Polish on the web. The app's detection diverges from the web unless the full LocaleList is read.

Greek (el) and Bulgarian (bg) render entirely in system fallback fonts. Their rows in the language list (Ελληνικά, Български) will look different from the Hanken rows, and display titles lose Bricolage. The web has the same gap; the brand impact needs an owner decision.

Mixed-language screens: advisor roles, bios, greetings and specialties, review quotes, season copy (English by contract) and the session markers stay English inside a translated UI. Session-marker colour is inferred from the English word 'started', so translating markers on the server would silently break it.

Translated copy is longer than English (German often about 30% longer). Layouts sized for English, the server-checked English length limits on season texts (hero title 26 chars) and fixed row heights (the CountryPickerSheet's 48pt + getItemLayout pattern) can clip, especially at large Dynamic Type, which the app never caps.

VoiceOver reads an in-app language that differs from the device language with the device's voice, unless an app-wide accessibility language is set natively. RN's own role and state words always follow the OS language, and Android TalkBack has no per-element language support in RN.

Background push notifications are rendered in a fresh headless JS context. If that path does not read the stored preference before building the text, notifications come out in the device or source language instead of the chosen one.

OS-drawn surfaces (iOS permission prompts via InfoPlist.strings, App Store / Google Play purchase sheets, Android notification-channel settings) follow the OS language, not the in-app choice. A user who picks a language different from the device's sees two languages.

Without a 'Device language' option, the first explicit choice pins the app to that language forever, even after the phone's language changes, with no way back to automatic (the web has exactly this behaviour).

Android has allowBackup=false and iOS reinstall without a backup restore starts clean, so the explicit choice is lost on reinstall. The fallback to device language is usually right; storing the choice under Caches would also let the OS purge it.
Bringing back the Advisors globe/EN pill would recreate the AURAT-0041 stub, and on Advisors it would read as an advisor-language filter, which is what the web handoff means by 'Language' there.

Sending Accept-Language (assumption 9) has no UX effect today because the BFF ignores it. It creates an implicit contract that the server may later honour inconsistently (cached, server-localized content would then need refetching on a switch).
recommendations: Step 1, ship gate: keep the runtime language forced to 'en' and the Language row hidden behind one flag until every user-visible string is extracted in all 24 languages. Then turn on detection and the picker in the same release. Tests can render other languages before that.

Step 2, preference model: one per-device value, 'device' (the default; nothing stored) or an explicit Language. Resolve 'device' from the device's ordered preferred-language list, taking the first supported base code (de-AT → de, pt-BR → pt, es-419 → es), else English, as the web does (WEB detect-language.ts:11-19). Read the full list: iOS Settings.get('AppleLanguages'), Android LocaleList through the existing DeviceCountryModule. The single-value I18nManager/Intl locale is not enough. Resolve before first paint so the splash TAGLINE never flips.

Step 3, persistence: write only an explicit choice, atomically, to a durable app file (Documents/Application Support on iOS, filesDir on Android; never Caches, which the OS can purge). Keep it across sign-out and account deletion, since it is a device setting like the web's localStorage. Do not send it to the BFF and do not add a profile field. Revisit an account-level preferredLanguage only when the server starts writing user-facing text (email, server-rendered push, localized markers).

Step 4, Profile row: restore it in the design's position, after Coupons & Promo Codes and before Terms (README.md:216-224), with globe icon and tint #C9B6E4. Label it 'Language', singular as on the web (the design says 'Languages'; owner to confirm). The value is the autonym of the language in effect (e.g. 'Deutsch'), also in Device mode. Replace the 'any sheet row is wallet UI' filter with an explicit walletOnly flag on the promo row. Add an optional value slot to ProfileMenu (13.5, ink3, before the chevron), set accessibilityValue={{text: value}}, and key rows by id instead of label.

Step 5, sheet shell: restore the AURAF-0001 LanguageSheet (git show 1f65d57^:src/screens/profile/ui/LanguageSheet.tsx) inside screens/profile, where it has one consumer, like the web's pages/me, and modernise it. Use BottomSheet with dragFromGrip. Header: title 'Choose language' (display 700, 22/26, flex:1 so it wraps) plus the design's ✕ (34pt paper2 disc, x 18, hitSlop 5 to reach 44pt, translated 'Close'). Body: a ScrollView bounded to about 55-60% of window height, with the indicator shown (persistentScrollbar on Android, flashScrollIndicators() on open for iOS) and a partly visible last row as the scroll cue. 'Choose' is pinned below the list. Use fontFace(...), never fontWeight.

Step 6, row content and order: 'Device language' first (label in UI language, hint = autonym of the resolved language), then English, then the other 23 by autonym from one static config array that does not depend on the UI language: Български, Čeština, Dansk, Deutsch, Eesti, Ελληνικά, Español, Français, Gaeilge, Hrvatski, Italiano, Latviešu, Lietuvių, Magyar, Malti, Nederlands, Polski, Português, Română, Slovenčina, Slovenščina, Suomi, Svenska (Greek and Bulgarian placed by transliteration). Each row shows the autonym (16/600 ink) and, when different, the name in the current UI language as a hint (13.5 ink3), like the web's label + hint. Drop the design's regional variants. Rows use minHeight 54 with natural, wrapping height (no fixed heights, no getItemLayout), the design's 24pt radio, and React.memo with a stable onPress.

Step 7, commit semantics: keep the design's draft + 'Choose'. In a scrolled 24-row list, an instant switch on a mis-tap would flip the whole UI, including the sheet, into a language the user may not read. Reset the draft to the current preference on every open (TopUpSheet / old LanguageSheet pattern). ✕, scrim, swipe and Android back cancel. 'Choose' with an unchanged draft just closes. On open, scroll the selected row into view without animation, via the row's onLayout y.

Step 8, switch behaviour: on 'Choose', store the pending language and close the sheet. In BottomSheet.onClosed, apply it with i18n changeLanguage, and keep the old language on screen until the strings are ready. Re-render in place: no navigation remount, no reset, no splash, no restart; the user stays on Profile and watches it change. Announce the change for screen readers (AccessibilityInfo.announceForAccessibility, in the new language).

Step 9, native and system coherence, applied at the same moment: Firebase auth().setLanguageCode(effective) before any OTP request so the SMS matches the UI. Recreate Android notification channels with the same id so their names update. Declare the 24 localizations (CFBundleLocalizations / localeConfig) so iOS and Android per-app language settings exist and feed 'Device language'. Accept and document that iOS permission prompts and store sheets follow the OS language.

Step 10, first launch: no prompt and no onboarding step, following the design (ONBOARDING.md:18-22) and the web (picker is signed-in only). Detection sets the language from the first frame. Keep the subtitle 'You can change this later in your profile.' only for a future pre-auth entry. Either drop it in the Profile context or replace it with a scope line, at the owner's choice. Possible later additions, owner's call: a globe pill on the wizard's top bar, or a one-time sheet only for devices whose language fell back to English.

Step 11, Advisors: do not restore the globe/EN pill as part of i18n. It has no behaviour in the design, duplicates Profile as a static indicator, and the web handoff uses 'Language' there to mean advisor spoken language, for which the contract has no data.

Step 12, accessibility: wrap the list in accessibilityRole='radiogroup' labelled by the title. Rows get accessibilityRole='radio' with accessibilityState={{checked}} (not selected: checked gives 'radio button, checked/unchecked' on iOS and a checkable RadioButton on Android). Set accessibilityLabel to the autonym (plus the localized name when different) and, on iOS, accessibilityLanguage={code} on autonym rows, mirroring the web's lang on the label; check on a device that the role and state words stay intelligible. Mark server English content with accessibilityLanguage='en' when the UI is not English (web parity: season-ticket lang='en'). Translate the BottomSheet scrim label, add translated tab-bar labels, never cap font scaling, and set the native iOS app-wide accessibility language when the in-app language differs from the device's (unverified).

Step 13, fonts: decide bg/el explicitly. Either accept system fallback (cheapest; the web already does it) or bundle a Greek+Cyrillic companion face used only when the language is bg or el. Make sure every Latin-script language keeps Hanken/Bricolage; they are fully covered.

Step 14, server content: state in the spec that v1 localizes the UI only. Advisor bios and greetings, review quotes, season copy and session markers stay English, as on the web. Session-marker colour must not depend on translated wording; keep the BFF debt for a machine-readable marker kind.

Step 15, tests: update ProfileScreen.test.tsx:88 and AdvisorsScreen.test.tsx:96-98. Add tests for: the row shown with billing off; the value = autonym; draft reset on open; commit only on Choose; apply after onClosed; Device-mode resolution order; checked accessibility state.
