findings.summary: At the type level, the web's i18n core ports to the app almost unchanged. Translation<typeof en> plus a per-slice ResourceNamespaceMap augmentation (i18next 26) compiles under @react-native/typescript-config with the TS 5.9.3 the app actually has installed. A missing key, an extra key, a missing plural _other form, an unknown t() key and a wrong or missing interpolation variable (when an options object is passed) are all compile errors (verified). The loader and the init step must change for RN, though. Draft item 1 is refuted in its loader detail: in release Metro bundles every language anyway, and asyncRequire only wraps a synchronous require in a promise. In dev, RN asks for lazy=true bundles, so import() becomes a network fetch from Metro. The recommended shape is a synchronous typed thunk, de: () => (require('./de') as typeof import('./de')).default. It was verified to stay lazy after the RN Babel preset plus Metro inline-requires, to fail typecheck with TS2307 when the file is missing, and to pass the app's ESLint. There is a review trap: a default or namespace import of a translation file compiles to _interopRequireDefault(require()) at module top, and inlineRequires (on by default) does not move it. Every language would then execute at startup, measured at about +2 MB of Hermes heap. When resources are passed inline with initAsync: false, i18next 26 init and changeLanguage run synchronously with zero setTimeout calls. That removes any startup async gap and works with the app's global jest.useFakeTimers(). Draft items 2 and 3 are confirmed and sharpened: the shipped Hermes 250829098.0.10 exposes only Intl.getCanonicalLocales, Collator, DateTimeFormat and NumberFormat, on iOS (checked by running it) and on Android (checked in the libhermesvm.so string table). Without a polyfill, i18next silently applies English one/other rules to all 23 languages (verified on Hermes), and DisplayNames is missing entirely, not just unreliable. The draft's polyfill choice is refuted: intl-pluralrules@2.0.1 was last released in 2023 and disagrees with CLDR 48 (lv for 1000 and up, es/fr/it/pt for 1e6 and up). @formatjs/intl-pluralrules, as the conditional polyfill.js plus 24 locale-data files (about +125 KB of bytecode), matched Node ICU on Hermes, and a shim built on make-plural@8.2.0 is the lean alternative (about 21 KB). Bundling all 23 extra languages at web size costs about +1.04 MB of Hermes bytecode (+30% on the current 3.47 MB bundle, which the APK stores uncompressed; about +0.32 MB gzipped). On top of that comes about +0.45 MB of heap to register roughly 900 lazy modules, and about +0.1 MB per language actually executed. That is acceptable, so translations do not need to be downloaded over the air, but lazy loading is mandatory. Typecheck cost at web scale (39 namespaces, about 650 typed t() calls) is about +1.6 s and +290 MB over the app's 3.1 s baseline. The selector API halves that and grows linearly (at 78 namespaces: 1.65 s versus 5.1 s), so string keys are fine to start with. Raw strings can be forbidden mechanically: eslint-plugin-i18next 6.1.5 runs on the app's ESLint 8.57.1 and @react-native config. Its jsx-only mode gives 304 low-noise hits for ui/, and the type-aware 'all' mode covers copy in model/lib/config (527 hits, about 5% noise, lint time 3.4 s to 5.8 s). Lint is currently at 0 errors and 0 warnings, so adopt the rule as off by default with 'error' per migrated slice, not as a global warn. The RN Jest environment has full ICU 78.2 / CLDR 48. The web's completeness test, polyfill-equivalence tests and CLDR drift tests therefore run in Jest, and handlers that throw on missing keys or missing interpolation values cover what the types miss. The biggest hidden risk is formatting on Hermes: formatRange is missing, NumberFormat unit style is wrong (10 minutes comes out as '600 Sekunden'), compact/signDisplay/narrowSymbol are ignored, and date names differ from Node in 6 of 216 cells. The web's date, money and country-name helpers cannot be ported as they are. Instead, use per-language CLDR tables baked at authoring time from Node, guarded by drift tests, plus i18next plural keys for durations and relative days. The web's 23 languages were written by the agent within the task, without native review. They give only about 24% exact translation-memory matches for the app's strings, and they show register drift (Bulgarian mixes formal and informal) and term drift (French and Portuguese 'chat'). Reusing them needs a glossary and consistency pass. A side finding for draft item 5: on Apple Hermes the default Intl locale follows the region-format setting (AppleLocale), not the preferred-languages list, so Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().locale is not a reliable UI-language signal.

In release builds import() inside the single bundle runs require.importAll synchronously inside an async function (no separate chunk). In dev, RN requests lazy=true bundles and installs __loadBundleAsync=loadBundleFromServer, so import() becomes a network fetch from Metro. Dev and release behave differently.

A default import becomes var _de = _interopRequireDefault(require('./de')) at module top (eager). A namespace import becomes _interopRequireWildcard at top (eager). () => require('./de').default and () => (require('./de') as typeof import('./de')).default stay lazy.

Hermes has no DateTimeFormat.prototype.formatRange. NumberFormat style:'unit' misformats: de minute long 10 -> '600 Sekunden', pl minute short 5 -> '300s', fr kilobyte -> '248 kilobyte'. notation:'compact', signDisplay and currencyDisplay:'narrowSymbol' are ignored. timeZoneName, hourCycle:'h23', hour12:false, dateStyle, percent, Collator, toLocaleUpperCase and normalize work.

On Hermes (desktop), constructing an Intl formatter per call costs about 88 us (NumberFormat) and 50 us (DateTimeFormat), against about 1 us with a cached instance; a baked-table string assembly costs about 8.5 us.

Baking per-language CLDR date patterns, month/weekday names and the USD format from Node takes about 1 KB per language (24 KB for 24 languages). The drift check (43,968 comparisons against Node Intl) immediately caught two CLDR details a naive table misses: Lithuanian numeric zero-padded day+month ('06-02'), and minimumGroupingDigits=2 for bg, es, et, hu, it, lv, pl, sl ('1234,50' but '99 999,99'). CLDR short months are numeric for bg and lt ('06').

App formatting is hand-written English. shared/lib/format.ts formats USD as '$'+toFixed(2) and a 24-hour clock 'on purpose' because of Hermes toLocaleTimeString variance. shared/lib/dates.ts and screens/home/lib/format-date.ts hold duplicate English WEEKDAYS/MONTHS tables. relativeDay returns 'Today'/'Tomorrow'/'In N days'; formatMinutes returns 'N min'; untilLabel returns 'in N h M min'; discount-copy returns '% OFF'. countries.ts bakes English country names because DisplayNames is unreliable on Hermes.
The web's formatters depend on Intl APIs Hermes lacks: formatTimeRange uses formatRange, languageName and the phone country list use Intl.DisplayNames. They cannot be ported to the app as they are.

Localised country names baked from Node CLDR for the app's 245 countries x 23 languages come to about 108 KB of JSON (about 4.7 KB per language, loadable per language). CLDR autonyms are lower-case in many languages (español, français, čeština) and need capitalising for a list.
facts.evidence: node Intl.DisplayNames run over iso2 codes parsed from APP/src/shared/config/countries.ts

facts.claim: pseudo-localization 3.1.3 (ESM-only) corrupts i18next placeholders ('In {{count}} days' -> 'Īƞ {{ƈǿǿŭŭƞŧ}} ḓȧȧẏş'). i18next-pseudo 2.2.1 was last published in 2022.

i18next-cli 1.82.4 bundles extract/types/status/lint (hardcoded strings) but targets JSON locale files and pulls heavy dependencies (@swc/core). The TS-module + satisfies design already gives completeness, so it is optional.
The Hermes macOS slice used for the runtime probes runs the same Apple Foundation-based Intl implementation as iOS, and Android's Java ICU-based Intl behaves like it for currency and date options.
facts.evidence: Inferred from identical version and the Apple-style behaviour (e.g. unit normalisation); Android Hermes was not executed, only its string table was inspected

facts.claim: Bytecode of unexecuted language modules costs little resident memory because Hermes mmaps the uncompressed bundle and only touched pages are loaded.
facts.evidence: APK stores the bundle uncompressed (verified); RSS behaviour on device was not measured

risks: The default-import trap: `import de from './de'` (or `import * as`) in a namespace index executes every language at startup. Measured at +2.0 MB Hermes heap and startup CPU, it passes typecheck and tests silently. It needs a lint guard and review attention.
A plain `require('./xx')` loader loses the compile-time 'file exists' check (verified: deleting mt.ts gives no tsc error). Only Metro bundling or the Jest completeness test would catch it.

Porting the web's helpers as they are breaks on Hermes: formatRange is undefined (throws), Intl.DisplayNames is undefined, and NumberFormat unit/compact/signDisplay/narrowSymbol misrender (10 minutes -> '600 Sekunden').

Without a PluralRules polyfill, every non-English plural is silently wrong (one/other only). If the device polyfill's CLDR version drifts from Node's CLDR 48 used by the completeness test, categories can mismatch, and a missing form falls back to English _other.
Choosing intl-pluralrules@2.0.1, as the draft suggested, ships known CLDR mismatches (lv for 1000 and up, es/fr/it/pt for 1e6 and up) from a package unmaintained since 2023-07.

@formatjs/intl-pluralrules and make-plural are ESM-only. Importing them from a module that Jest loads fails unless they are added to transformIgnorePatterns, so keep the polyfill import in index.js only.

Very fresh releases (i18next 26.7.1 at 3 days, react-i18next 17.1.12 at 1 day, @formatjs/intl-pluralrules 7.0.x as a new major at 4 days) carry regression risk. Prefer the web's 26.5.3/17.1.0 and formatjs 6.3.16 until the newer ones age.

Android Hermes Intl output was not executed here, only its API surface. Runtime-Intl formatting may differ between iOS and Android and across Android ICU versions. Baked CLDR tables remove that class of 'different text on two phones' bug.
TypeScript cost with string keys grows superlinearly with namespace count (78 namespaces: 5.1 s check, 443 MB). IDE/tsserver memory pressure may appear before CI time does.
The type-aware 'all' lint mode needs parserOptions.project (lint 3.4 s -> 5.8 s) and some tuning of callee/property/word excludes. Untyped 'all' mode is unusable (1603 mostly false hits).
A global 'warn' level would end the current 0-warning lint baseline (300-600 warnings) and bury real signals.

jest.setup.js must not import slice public APIs, because that preloads api/model modules before test-file jest.mock calls (the web hit the vi.mock analogue). Locale index files must keep only type-only imports of @/shared.

Translations produced by an agent without native review, in payment, refund, cancellation, account-deletion and legal flows, risk misleading consumers in EU markets. Whether local-language consumer-law obligations apply was not checked.

Reusing web translation memory as is spreads the web's inconsistencies (Bulgarian register mix; French/Portuguese 'chat' vs 'discussion'/'conversa') and can let the two clients drift unless one glossary governs both.

Latvian _zero is a grammatical category (0, 10-20, 30, ...), not 'none'. i18next uses _zero for count 0 whenever the key exists, so a translator adding _zero in another language changes output. The completeness test must enforce exact CLDR category sets (as the web's does).
Text expansion (short-label p95 1.6-2.2x, max 5.5x) will truncate fixed-width tabs, buttons and pills, especially in ga, fr, el, de, hu and lt.
CLDR short months are numeric for bg and lt ('06'), so the calendar-block design (day number over 'Jun') looks odd unless overridden.

Per-slice x language files mean about 900 extra Metro modules (+~0.45 MB heap at registration, 1,840 -> about 2,740 modules). On low-end Android devices the startup cost may become measurable. Not measured on a device.
recommendations: Step 1 — dependencies. Add i18next 26.5.3 and react-i18next 17.1.0 (the web's versions, both over two weeks old; i18next 26.5.3 was verified on Hermes with sync init) and @formatjs/intl-pluralrules 6.3.16 (move to 7.0.2 or later once it has aged; 7.0.2 matched CLDR 48 exactly). Add eslint-plugin-i18next 6.1.5 as a devDependency. Do not add intl-pluralrules, i18next-pseudo, pseudo-localization or @formatjs/intl-displaynames.

Step 2 — core types. Copy the web's shared/config/languages.ts and shared/i18n/namespace.ts verbatim (LANGUAGES, Translation<Source>, PluralCategory). Change only the loader type to synchronous: load: Readonly<Record<TranslatedLanguage, () => Translation<Source>>>.

Step 3 — slice layout. Each slice keeps config/locales/{en.ts as const, <lang>.ts default export satisfies Translation<typeof en>, index.ts}, as on the web. In index.ts, import './en' at runtime, import @/shared types only (import type), and write loaders as `bg: () => (require('./bg') as typeof import('./bg')).default`. This was verified to stay lazy, type-check the file's shape and existence, and pass the app's ESLint. Never default-import or namespace-import a non-English locale file.

Step 4 — synchronous init. initI18nSync(namespaces, language) calls i18next.use(initReactI18next).init({lng, fallbackLng:'en', supportedLngs:LANGUAGES, load:'languageOnly', ns, defaultNS:false, resources:{en: sources, [lng]: ns.load[lng]()}, initAsync:false, interpolation:{escapeValue:false}, returnNull:false, react:{useSuspense:false}}). chooseLanguage(lng) calls addResourceBundle(lng, ns.name, ns.load[lng](), true, true) for each namespace, then changeLanguage (synchronous). No splash wait is needed for strings.

Step 5 — plurals on Hermes. As the first lines of index.js (never in modules under test), import '@formatjs/intl-pluralrules/polyfill.js' plus the 24 locale-data/<lang>.js files. This is conditional: it installs on Hermes and keeps the native implementation in Jest. Add a Jest equivalence test comparing the polyfill's PluralRules with Node's native one for 0..1000 and a few decimals across all 24 languages. If the bundle budget is tight, swap in a ~30-line make-plural 8.2.0 shim (about 21 KB of bytecode, exact cardinals) guarded by the same test.

Step 6 — Jest. In jest.setup.js, require i18next and react-i18next and each <slice>/config/locales directly (not public APIs). Init English synchronously with initAsync:false, and set saveMissing:true with a missingKeyHandler and a missingInterpolationHandler that throw, which catches t('key') calls without options that the types allow. Add an ESLint override turning no-restricted-imports off for jest.setup.js. Port the web test asserting that the setup's namespace list equals I18N_NAMESPACES. Existing English assertions keep passing if en.ts reproduces today's strings exactly.

Step 7 — QA suite. Port the web's app/config/__tests__/i18n.test.ts (keys, blanks, placeholder parity, exact CLDR plural categories via Node Intl) and extend it with: (a) a check for strings identical to English, using a global allowlist (Aura, Apple Pay, Google Play, App Store, placeholder/punctuation-only strings) plus per-language loanword allowlists; (b) length-ratio warnings (short strings over 2.0x English, others over 1.8x), and hard limits for keys with a declared budget (tab labels, buttons); (c) a do-not-translate brand check; (d) the polyfill equivalence test; (e) drift tests for the baked CLDR tables; (f) a guard that no config/locales/index.ts statically imports a non-English file.

Step 8 — ESLint gates. Keep i18next/no-literal-string off globally to preserve the 0-warning baseline. For each migrated slice, add overrides: ui/**/*.tsx with mode 'jsx-only', should-validate-template true, jsx-attributes excludes for RN non-text props (testID, name, variant, size, tone, style, *Style, *Color, keyboardType, autoComplete, textContentType, returnKeyType, accessibilityRole, role, resizeMode, pointerEvents, hitSlop, animationType*, submitBehavior, ...) and word excludes for brands and punctuation; model/lib/config (excluding config/locales/**) with mode 'all' plus parserOptions.project and tuned callee excludes (t, bffRequest, Error, Date, fontFace, require, console.*) and object-property excludes (displayName, id, key, kind, type, status). Track the backlog with a separate script, not with npm run lint. Flip to a global 'error' once the last slice is migrated.

Step 9 — formatting. Add one shared module (for example shared/lib/i18n-format.ts) that receives the language explicitly. It is backed by per-language CLDR tables generated by a Node script (full ICU): month names in format and standalone context, weekday long/short, patterns for the app's date shapes (long date, day+month, month block, weekday short, home eyebrow) and the USD money format (symbol, decimal, group, minimumGroupingDigits, pattern). Load the tables with the language (about 1 KB per language), and check them with a Jest drift test, as countries.ts already does. Put durations ('10 min', 'in 2 h 10 min') and relative days in i18next plural keys, reusing the web's relative.* and duration.minutes_* keys. Keep formatClockTime and formatCountdown language-neutral. Fold the duplicate WEEKDAYS/MONTHS tables in shared/lib/dates.ts and screens/home/lib/format-date.ts into this module. Never use formatRange, DisplayNames, RelativeTimeFormat, NumberFormat unit, compact, signDisplay or narrowSymbol on Hermes. If runtime Intl is used anywhere, cache formatter instances per language and option set.

Step 10 — names lists. Bake language autonyms (24 entries, capitalised as list items) and, if the owner wants localised country names in the phone picker, per-language country-name tables (about 4.7 KB per language, loaded per language) from Node CLDR, with a test that the generator output is up to date. Sort at runtime with Intl.Collator, which works on Hermes.

Step 11 — glossary and register. Seed a machine-readable glossary from the web's aligned files (82 short domain strings, for example advisor, session, reading, balance, top up, promo code, tarot, free chat, reschedule) with the agreed term per language, part of speech and register. Resolve the 78 within-language divergences once. Make the register table explicit for all 23 languages: the web's policy plus it, pl, mt, ga, which are de facto informal. Use one glossary for both clients and fix web drift in the same pass.

Step 12 — translation memory and production. For each new app string, prefill from exact web matches (about 24% of strings) after the glossary pass, then have the implementing task translate the rest into all 23 languages in the same task (the web's hard rule 9). Run the QA suite. Record each language and namespace in a review ledger in the brain (machine/agent vs native-reviewed, date). Mark strings in payments, refunds, cancellation, account deletion and legal copy as requiring native review before marketing in a market.

Step 13 — pseudo-locale. In __DEV__ only, add a pseudo language generated at init from the English resources: accent map, about 40% padding (above the measured median expansion of 1.04-1.26 and near the long-string p95), and brackets that reveal clipping. It must leave {{...}} tokens untouched; write it in-house because pseudo-localization 3.1.3 corrupts them. Expose it only from a dev menu, and in dev set parseMissingKeyHandler to show a marked key so missing keys are visible.

Step 14 — bundle policy. Ship all 24 languages in the bundle (about +1.0-1.3 MB of bytecode, or about +1.3-1.6 MB with i18next, the polyfill and country names; about +0.3-0.45 MB compressed download). Load lazily via the require thunks, and record the bundle size per release in manor. Revisit per-language aggregated modules (which removes about 0.45 MB of registration heap) only if device measurements show startup or memory pressure.

Step 15 — keys versus selectors. Start with string keys and useTranslation('<ns>') for parity with the web (about +1.6 s typecheck at web scale). Switch the app to enableSelector: true (verified to keep key and interpolation checks, about 2-3x cheaper at 78 namespaces) if tsc or tsserver time becomes a problem. Never use 'optimize', which breaks plural base keys.
open_questions_for_owner: Register per language: adopt the web's informal/formal table for the app, and confirm it, pl, mt and ga as informal (the web's de facto choice)? Which form should Bulgarian use, given the web currently mixes 'Резервирай' and 'Резервирайте'?
Clock: keep the app's fixed 24-hour '16:05' in every language, or follow CLDR as the web does (en '4:05 PM', el 12-hour, da/fi '16.05')? Should app and web agree?

Native-speaker review: keep the web's 'welcome, non-blocking' rule, or make review blocking for payment, refund, cancellation, account-deletion and legal strings before the app is marketed in a given country?
Bundle budget: is about +1.3-1.6 MB of Hermes bytecode (about +40% over today's 3.47 MB) acceptable for shipping all 24 languages in the binary?
Should the phone-country picker show localised country names at launch (about 4.7 KB per language), or stay English for now?
String-key t('a.b') for parity with the web, or the selector API t($ => $.a.b) for faster typechecks in the app?
Bulgarian and Lithuanian CLDR short months are numeric ('06'): accept that in the calendar blocks, or supply custom abbreviations?
Where should the shared glossary and translation memory for app and web live (brain, or a shared file or package), and should fixing web translation drift be part of the app's i18n work?
Should the dev pseudo-locale also be available in internal staging builds, or in dev builds only?

contradictions: [RESOLVED, see resolved_checks #1] iOS default Intl locale. tooling-quality says Apple Hermes 'follows AppleLocale (region format), not AppleLanguages' (-AppleLanguages (de-DE) gives en-US; -AppleLocale fr_FR gives fr-FR), so Intl is 'not a reliable UI-language signal'. hermes-intl and native-platform say the opposite: the language is AppleLanguages best-matched against the bundle's localizations, and only the region comes from AppleLocale. tooling-quality's host was a bare executable with no .app bundle, so no bundle matching ran. Re-running the same Hermes inside .app bundles confirms hermes-intl and native-platform. tooling-quality's conclusion holds only for today's English-only bundle, where the language is always 'en'.

Plural polyfill choice. hermes-intl recommends a vendored 24-language shim on make-plural pinned to 8.1.0: 0 of 55,560 mismatches, about 3 KB gzipped, about 1.3 µs per select. It rejects @formatjs/intl-pluralrules: about 190 µs per select on desktop Hermes (about 75x slower), and it throws for any locale without loaded data unless @formatjs/intl-locale (+77 KB gzipped) is added. tooling-quality recommends @formatjs/intl-pluralrules 6.3.16 (conditional polyfill plus 24 locale-data files, about 125 KB of bytecode) with the shim only as a fallback, and it uses make-plural 8.2.0, published 2026-10-25 and only 10 days old. tooling-quality measured neither the per-select cost nor the unloaded-locale throw. The two also report different ordinal results: formatjs 7.0.2 has 0 mismatches per tooling-quality but 110 bg/es ordinal mismatches per hermes-intl, and make-plural 8.2.0 ordinals differ for bg/es while 8.1.0 matches ICU 78.2. That comes from a cardinal-only sweep plus a CLDR data change. Ordinals are unused (the web has no ordinal keys). On the evidence, the make-plural 8.1.0 shim is the better choice.

intl-pluralrules@2.0.1 error count: hermes-intl found 1,614 of 55,560 wrong (lt, lv, mt and ro for 1000 and up; es/fr/it/pt at 1e6), tooling-quality found 13 (lv for 1000 and up; es/fr/it/pt for 1e6 and up). The sample sets differ: tooling-quality tested 0..1000 plus a few large values and missed lt/ro/mt above 1000. Both reject the package, so there is no impact on the decision.

How the BFF learns the language. native-platform STEP 6c: send 'Accept-Language: <lang>' from APP/src/shared/api/bff/http-client.ts:60 and upload.ts:79. backend-contracts: append an explicit `lang` query parameter instead, and have the BFF deliberately ignore Accept-Language, because shipped iOS builds already send an implicit device-language Accept-Language (checked only with a macOS CFNetwork probe) and browsers send their own. web-i18n and design-ux: do nothing for now, since the BFF ignores it. Server tolerance of an extra query parameter is now verified (resolved_checks #8). What remains to decide is whether requests from old iOS builds must be told apart from new ones. Only an explicit parameter does that; a custom header would also do it, but needs a CORS change for the web.

Where the language choice is stored. backend-contracts: a users.language column, plus a language field on ProfileResponse and ProfilePatchRequest and a desk attribute. ProfilePatchRequest is .strict(), so the BFF must deploy first. design-ux: per device only, never sent to the BFF, matching the web, where the profile has no language field. web-i18n: left to the owner. This is owner decision D3, and it also determines the privacy-policy wording.

How the choice persists. native-platform: on Android, store it only as the OS per-app locale (AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales plus AppLocalesMetadataHolderService, with a SharedPreferences mirror on API 32 and below for headless starts). On iOS, store an override {language, osLanguage} in Documents and drop it when the OS (bundle-matched) language changes, so the newest change wins. design-ux: one per-device file on both platforms (Documents/Application Support, filesDir) holding 'device' or an explicit language, which stays until the user picks 'Device language'. app-strings: a file in Documents/Library. The models behave differently after an iOS Settings or device-language change, and only the first integrates with Android Settings. The panel must pick one.

Where the device language comes from. On iOS, design-ux reads Settings.get('AppleLanguages') and takes the first supported base code. hermes-intl and native-platform take the language subtag of Intl's default locale, which after CFBundleLocalizations ships is Apple's bundle matching and also reflects the iOS per-app language. On Android, design-ux extends DeviceCountryModule to return the LocaleList. native-platform adds a new AuraAppLocale module (LocaleManager applicationLocales/systemLocales plus an AppCompat setter). hermes-intl relies on localeFilters plus values-<lang> resources (including ga and mt) so that Intl's resource-negotiated default can be used. The approaches agree in common cases but differ for per-app settings and for ga and mt.

Greek and Bulgarian fonts. design-ux Step 13 suggests 'a Greek+Cyrillic companion face used only when the language is bg or el'. fonts-glyphs shows that swapping faces per language through fontFace() cannot take effect on a runtime switch: there are 207 fontFace() calls, and 91 files evaluate them inside module-level StyleSheet.create. It would also miss user-written chat text and cost about 290-790 KB. fonts-glyphs instead recommends a build-time glyph merge under the same PostScript names (about +143 KB) or accepting the system fallback. app-strings says Greek/Cyrillic builds were 'not checked'. fonts-glyphs did check: upstream Hanken has Greek since commit eff37d18 (no Cyrillic), and Bricolage has neither.
[RESOLVED, see resolved_checks #12] Hanken Greek glyphs. app-strings: 'Hanken has only the math glyphs μ and Δ'. fonts-glyphs: Δ Ω μ π plus Greek punctuation. fc-query confirms fonts-glyphs.

[RESOLVED, see resolved_checks #2] String.prototype.normalize on Hermes. web-i18n Step 7 says not to call Intl.DisplayNames or String.normalize at runtime; tooling-quality says normalize works. It works on both platforms, and the app already calls it at runtime. Pre-folding is a performance choice, not an availability one.

[RESOLVED, see resolved_checks #4] Hermes toLocaleUpperCase('el'). fonts-glyphs: unknown on Hermes (only V8 was checked). hermes-intl: drops accents on Hermes/Apple. Confirmed on Apple by running it, and on Android from bytecode (android.icu UCharacter.toUpperCase(ULocale)).

[QUALIFIED, see resolved_checks #3] Collator. hermes-intl: 'Collator and localeCompare work and follow each language's sort rules' on Hermes/Apple. That is true only for the default sensitivity. With sensitivity 'base', the Apple build ignores language-specific letters and is inconsistent: in Swedish a==ä but ä>z, so a sorted list comes out wrong.

Formatting strategy. tooling-quality: never rely on runtime Intl for display. Bake per-language CLDR tables instead (month and weekday names, date patterns, USD pattern, minimumGroupingDigits) with drift tests against Node; Apple differs from Node in 6 of 216 date cells, and Android (ICU4J, CLDR 28 on API 24) was never run. hermes-intl: a cached Intl.NumberFormat gives USD byte-identical to V8 for all 24 languages on Apple, and Intl.DateTimeFormat month and weekday names come out right (nominative and genitive), so use them, avoiding the unit, compact, signDisplay, formatRange and timeZoneName options. app-strings: CLDR cannot produce the day-over-month blocks for bg/lt (numeric months) or cs/fi/hu (different order), so those need translated abbreviation tables either way. The locale passed differs too: native-platform STEP 6f passes `${lang}-${region}` to Intl, while the web and hermes-intl pass only the UI language.

Translation-memory reuse. web-i18n: 241 of 523 non-date app strings (46%) exactly match a web English string. tooling-quality: 224 of about 920 literals (24.3%). The matching counts agree; tooling-quality's denominator includes non-copy literals such as SVG paths. Plan effort on about 40-46% of the real copy being reusable.

Bundle cost. web-i18n: about +0.6 MB of Hermes bytecode, scaling the web's 986 KB for 24 languages by the app's 61% share of characters. tooling-quality: +1.04 MB at web size, or +1.3-1.6 MB including i18next and react-i18next (122 KB), the plural polyfill (21-125 KB) and country-name tables, plus about +0.45 MB of heap for about 900 lazy modules. State it as +0.6 to 1.6 MB; the polyfill choice alone moves it by about 100 KB.

Language sheet design. design-ux: keep design screen 15 (pick, then 'Choose'; no search; 'Device language' first; autonym plus hint; Greek and Bulgarian placed among the Latin names by transliteration). web-i18n: a searchable list like the autocomplete the owner asked for on the web (AURAT-0136-009), with the owner choosing instant switch or commit. The web lists languages in ISO-code order; hermes-intl sorted autonyms with Collator('en'), which puts Latin first and Greek/Cyrillic last. This is an owner decision. Whatever order is chosen should be a fixed array in config, not computed by a Collator at runtime (resolved_checks #3).

When to share the LANGUAGES list. backend-contracts STEP 2: move LANGUAGES, Language and SOURCE_LANGUAGE into @aura/contracts v0.28.0 now. web-i18n Step 14: only once server-side localization is scheduled. native-platform STEP 0: an app-local shared/config/languages.ts identical to the web's, plus a Jest test that locks five native lists to it.

Release gating. design-ux: keep the runtime language forced to 'en' behind a flag until every string exists in all 24 languages, then turn on detection and the picker in one release. First-draft item 7: extract layer by layer, with all 24 languages in each task. native-platform asks whether CFBundleLocalizations and localeConfig should ship only in that final release. These fit together only if the native declarations are gated too. Shipping CFBundleLocalizations early switches iOS system UI and permission prompts to the user's language, and per one forum report the App Store 'Languages' line to 24, while the app's own UI is still English.

Project context versus code. The shared context and .claude/aura-build-rules.md say the app uses Redux Toolkit/RTK Query. app-strings verified there is no redux or @reduxjs dependency; state lives in module-level stores read through useSyncExternalStore. The i18n plan must not assume Redux, for example by keeping the language in a Redux slice.

Count mismatches with no decision impact: Android library locale folders 86 (hermes-intl) vs 87 (native-platform); country rows 245 (app-strings, by grep) vs 246 (web-i18n); missing Bulgarian letters 60/62 (fonts-glyphs) vs 66 (design-ux). All agree that Cyrillic coverage is zero.
unverified_but_decision_critical: Android runtime behaviour has been checked only in source and bytecode, never on a device. That covers: the default locale being the OS best match against the APK's resource locales; Intl's default following it; AppCompat's per-app locale on API 32 and below, which loads only when an AppCompatActivity is created, so a headless FCM start sees none; LocaleManager on API 33 and up; per-app tags losing the region; AAB language splits; whether localeFilters 'pt' keeps values-pt-rPT; Hermes Intl output on ICU4J (CLDR 28 on API 24); and half-up rounding against iOS half-even. A device matrix in manor (API 24, 33 and 35) is needed before the detection and persistence design is frozen.

The iOS runtime claims rest on macOS stand-ins: bundle-matched Intl default locale (re-confirmed in this session, on macOS only); the contents of Settings.get('AppleLanguages'); when the per-app Language row appears (at least 2 app localizations and at least 2 user languages; the UIPrefersShowingLanguageSettings key is undocumented); iOS relaunching the app on a language change (forum answer); the system fallback face for el/bg (Helvetica on macOS CoreText, possibly San Francisco on iOS); and Apple Collator behaviour (resolved_checks #3 used the macOS 26.2 Foundation, while the app supports iOS 15.1-26).

Language of the Firebase OTP SMS. Two searches found no official list of SMS template languages. No one has verified template coverage for ga or mt (or any language), the project's current default template language, or that calling auth().setLanguageCode(code) before verifyPhoneNumber actually changes the SMS on both platforms. The SMS is the first translated thing a new user sees.

That iOS CFNetwork sends an implicit Accept-Language built from the device's first language even when the bundle is English-only ('de-DE,de;q=0.9') was measured only on macOS (backend-contracts, verified=false). It is the only argument for a `lang` query parameter over Accept-Language.

Nobody checked EU or national language law for consumer-facing text: Terms, Privacy, pre-contractual information, checkout, prices and refund/cancellation copy. Several member states have state-language laws for consumer dealings (from memory, not verified: France's Loi Toubon, Poland's Act on the Polish Language, Baltic and Slovak state-language acts). This decides whether English-only legal pages on aura-app.cc, agent-written payment and refund copy without native review, and USD prices shown next to EUR store prices are acceptable at launch in a given market.

That the App Store product page's 'Languages' line comes from the binary's .lproj folders rests on a single developer forum report (native-platform). It decides whether InfoPlist strings must ship for all 24 languages, and whether native declarations shipped early would advertise languages the app does not have yet.
